summary: The U.S. Space Force expects to spend an additional $17 billion on launch capabilities to meet surging demand, marking a significant expansion in defense space procurement. In commercial launch milestones, launch provider Isar Aerospace successfully reached orbit on its second attempt, while rocket developer Stoke Space raised $1 billion in Series E funding to advance its fully reusable launch system. Internationally, the United Kingdom outlined a $10.6 billion, four-year space plan with defense as a primary focus, while European leaders are urging closer cooperation among regional programs, including Galileo, Copernicus, and IRIS², to maintain competitiveness. In civil government and commercial Earth observation, NASA issued a call for technology proposals to accelerate lunar surface capabilities, and Earth imaging startup Pixxel secured $100 million in Series C funding for its next-generation satellite constellation. Scientific research made major strides as joint observations from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes revealed that distant solar system objects retain physical records of their early formation, a newly compiled supernova dataset began challenging established dark energy theories, and preliminary lab tests showed an eggshell-inspired aluminum material offers potential debris protection for spacecraft. Looking ahead, industry analysts and space enthusiasts will be watching Stoke Space as the company targets early 2027 for the debut launch of its fully reusable rocket.
